Case Information: A 13-year-old girl was admitted to our hospital with a history of persistent jaundice and skin itching for one month. She is the first child of a nonconsanguineous couple with no notable family history and was born healthy via normal delivery, weighing 3200 g at birth. No significant abnormalities were observed during the perinatal period. During infancy, she exhibited skin hyperkeratosis and mild limb bone abnormalities, which progressed to ichthyosis and pronounced claw-like hands and feet by the age of 6 years. Additionally, she experienced progressive itching and recurrent desquamation of the hands and feet since the age of 6. One month prior to admission, she sought medical attention at a local hospital due to worsening jaundice and severe skin itching. At the local hospital, she was found to have acute liver failure, cholestasis, hypoalbuminemia, and abnormal blood coagulation. She received various treatments, including hepatoprotective therapy, plasma exchange, albumin infusion, and methylprednisolone pulse therapy. Following these treatments, her liver function, hypoalbuminemia, and blood coagulation improved, but jaundice and skin itching persisted. The patient was then discharged after blood samples were taken for further genetic analysis.
Diagnostic Tests: WGS results revealed novel compound heterozygous mutations of VPS33B, c.1081 C > T (p.Q361X,257)/c.244 T > C (p. C82R), which was inherited from her father and mother as the parents are heterozygote carriers. Liver biopsy revealed the absence of the bile duct, and the gross bile ducts were severely dilated and filled with fine particles of bile. Electron microscopy showed hepatocytes of unequal size and disorganized arrangement with dilated hepatic sinuses. The mitochondria were swollen, the rough endoplasmic reticulum was hyperplastic and vesicular, the lysosomes were increased, and no viral particles were seen.

Case Information: An eight-year-old male patient from Morocco was referred for a medical genetics consultation due to the presence of distinctive facial features and multiple physical anomalies. He was born to a healthy consanguineous couple, with the mother aged 27 and the father aged 40. There is a family history of a sister who passed away at the age of three with similar symptoms. The pregnancy was not monitored medically but was reported to be uncomplicated. At birth, the patient weighed 2800g, measured 52cm in length, and had a head circumference of 36cm. His development appeared normal during the first month of life. At eight years old, clinical examination revealed delayed growth with a weight of 15kg (–3 standard deviation), height of 80cm (–4 standard deviation), and an Occipital Frontal Circumference of 52cm (mean). The patient exhibited joint contractures, painful diffusely thickened skin, hyperpigmentation over joints, papular and/or nodular skin lesions, and gingival hypertrophy. His cognitive development was reported to be normal.
Diagnostic Tests: His skin biopsy showed hyaline material accumulation in the dermis. Sequencing of the exon 13 of the CMG2 gene revealed a homozygous deletion in the exon 13 (c.1074delT; p.A359HfsX50).

Case Information: A 27-year-old male of Arabic descent visited the dermatology clinic with concerns about bilateral, symmetrical, hyperpigmented patches on his upper back. These patches had been present since birth, gradually increasing in size and darkening over the years, and were accompanied by the development of sparse hair on the affected areas. The patient reported no factors that relieved or worsened the condition, and there were no symptoms such as pain, itching, bleeding, or ulceration. A comprehensive review of systems, as well as the patient's medical, surgical, drug, and allergy history, revealed no abnormalities. There was no family history of skin diseases or other medical or congenital conditions, and the patient's four siblings had no similar complaints or skin issues. The patient's antenatal history included a normal vaginal delivery without complications, full-term birth, and up-to-date immunizations. The mother was healthy and did not take any medications during pregnancy. Examination of the body, hair, nails, and mucous membranes showed no abnormalities. The patient had not previously sought treatment for the lesions. On local skin examination, the hyperpigmented patches were found to be bilaterally symmetrical on the upper back, with the right patch measuring 15 × 7 cm and the left patch measuring 17 × 9 cm. Both patches were homogeneous and brown with irregular borders and blotchy hyperpigmented macules, and they were associated with sparse hair growth. The skin texture of the patches was similar to that of normal skin.
Diagnostic Tests: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and focal regular elongation of rete ridges with clubbing. There was increased basal layer pigmentation. The dermis revealed focal areas with pigment incontinence. There was no increase in smooth muscle in the dermis or hyperplasia of the hair follicles.

Case Information: A 12-year-old male from an Indian family of Dravidian origin exhibited progressive hair thinning over the past 2 years. He was born at term from a consanguineous marriage with sparse hair on the scalp, eyebrows, and eyelashes. Over time, his hair regrew as coarse and curly, but he experienced increased hair loss in the last 2 years. His natal and perinatal history were unremarkable, and his developmental milestones were achieved normally. There were no issues with sweating, and both personal and family medical histories were noncontributory. No systemic involvement was noted. On general physical examination, his vital signs were normal. The anterior hairline was receded and high. The scalp hair was coarse, dry, and wiry, standing out from the head. There was sparse hair with partial alopecia on the vertex, parietal, and occipital regions, resembling androgenetic alopecia. Eyebrows, eyelashes, and body hair were sparse. Examination of the palms, soles, and oral mucosa showed no abnormalities. Nails and teeth were normal, and systemic examination revealed no abnormalities.
Diagnostic Tests: Light microscopy of the hair shaft revealed darkly pigmented irregular twisting with variable diameters.

Case Information: A 19-month-old boy, born in March 2015, presented with multiple brown-black skin pigmentations on the face, trunk, and right leg, along with several smaller satellite lesions. He was brought to the hospital due to repeated vomiting over a period of 4 days. Physical examination revealed a round face, full cheeks, prominent forehead, widely spaced eyes, fullness around the eyes, a short nose, and an everted lower lip. The largest pigmented area was on the leg, measuring approximately 13 cm in diameter with additional measurements of (13 × 10), (8 × 6), and (4 × 2) cm.
Diagnostic Tests: Enhanced MRI showed hydrocephalus. The result of 6 months post-shunt MRI revealed the presence of supratentorial ventricular dilatation, brain stem volume reduction, in addition to leptomeningeal enhancement, however, no macroscopic mass was evident. Three months later, MRI showed a mass of 3 cm diameter, in the right frontal lobe. Pathological evaluation of CNS lesion, revealed that the mass was grossly dark-red to brown with the size of (4 × 4 × 2) cm. The tumor was firmly attached to the meninges. Microscopically, the tumor cells had atypical nuclei, obvious nucleoli, an increased karyoplasmic ratio, some mitoses, and remarkable necrosis, which infiltrated the brain parenchyma, accompanied with melanin deposition. The tumor cells were positively expressing the antibodies of HMB45, Melan-A, and S100. Ki-67 was positively expressed in 30% of the cells, while P53 was negative. Cytogenetic study revealed a lack of allelic deletion of P53. NRAS mutation in the third exon (codon 61), with a wild-type BRAFV600E.

Case Information: A 57-year-old Japanese woman presented with a 1-year history of a solitary erythematous plaque on the left leg. She had been treated with topical corticosteroid for a year without any improvement. The physical examination revealed a solitary erythematous plaque with a scaly surface measuring 17 × 14 mm in diameter. The dermoscopic examination demonstrated dotted and glomerular vessels with a homogenous pinkish background and whitish scaly areas. At the periphery of the lesion, there is a whitish negative network. The glomerular vessels are less prominent and the negative network is broader and more obscure. The whitish scaly areas are also less conspicuous.
Diagnostic Tests: The histopathological examination of an excisional biopsy disclosed massive band-like infiltrates of atypical lymphocytes with prominent epidermotropism within a hyperplastic epidermis. Atypical lymphocytes were positively stained with CD3 and predominantly with CD8, but negative with CD4, CD20, CD30, and CD79a.

Case Information: A 28-day-old female infant, the first child of non-consanguineous parents, was admitted to our hospital due to muscle weakness, neonatal seizures, and elevated serum very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) levels on March 19, 2018. She was delivered vaginally at 38 weeks and 2 days of gestation, with a birth weight of 2.21 kg. At birth, she presented with generalized muscle weakness and feeding difficulties, and experienced a seizure with low oxygen saturation one day post-birth. Despite normal results from her newborn screening, including tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), further metabolic evaluation for neonatal seizures showed elevated VLCFA levels: C26:0 was 11.47 μmol/L (normal range < 1.31 μmol/L); C24:0/C22:0 ratio was 2.21 (normal range < 1.39), and C26:0/C22:0 ratio was 0.5 (normal range < 0.023). Phytanic and pristanic acid levels were undetectable at 15 days of age. Physical examination revealed a high forehead, large anterior fontanel, midfacial underdevelopment, high-arched palate, low-set ears, and clubfoot.
Diagnostic Tests: The compound heterozygous mutations c.350A>T (p.Asp117Val) and c.836T>C (p.Phe279Ser), located in representative of 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency in HSD17B4 (NM_000414.3), were identified and inherited from the mother and father, respectively. The allele frequency of c.350A>T was 0.000109 in East Asian and c.836T>C have not reported yet.

Case Information: A 31-year-old male with end-stage renal disease due to chronic glomerulonephritis (IgA nephropathy) underwent a kidney transplant in December 2010 from a 25-year-old male donor who had experienced cardiac death following craniocerebral trauma. The patient had been on hemodialysis for one year before the transplant and had a history of tuberculosis contact and digestive tract hemorrhage. Preoperative chest X-rays, electrocardiograms, and echocardiography showed no abnormalities. Both the donor and recipient were seronegative for cytomegalovirus and hepatitis B and C viruses. The surgical follow-up was uneventful. The immunosuppressive regimen included 0.5 g intravenous methylprednisolone during surgery and 0.5 g/day for the first three days post-transplant. Tacrolimus was administered based on the patient's body weight of 65 kg at a dose of 6.5 mg/day for the initial three days, then adjusted according to the trough concentration to maintain levels of 6–8 ng/ml for the first six months and 5–6 ng/ml for months 6–12. Mycophenolate mofetil was given orally at 0.75 g every 12 hours, later reduced to 0.5 g every 12 hours for maintenance. Prednisolone was initially given at 80 mg/day and tapered over six months to 10 mg/day for long-term maintenance. The allograft functioned excellently immediately post-surgery. On day 11 post-transplant, the patient experienced chest pain, dyspnea, and a reduction in urinary output from over 2,000 ml/day to 1,000 ml/day. Physical examination revealed tachycardia, decreased systolic pressure, and jugular venous distention.
Diagnostic Tests: Echocardiography and chest computed tomography scans revealed an abundant compressive circumferential pericardial effusion (echo-free space, 62.3 mm) and pleural effusion with 49% of the left ventricular ejection fraction. Pericardiocentesis was performed and a lemon-colored exudative fluid (3,000 ml; protein level, 51.4 g/l; fluid/serum ratio, >0.5) with abundant polymorphonuclear cells was removed. Further investigations revealed that the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 6 mm/h, the serum creatinine level was 200 μmol/l, the serum lactate dehydrogenase level was 339.3 U/l (serum/fluid ratio, >0.6) and the adenosine deaminase level in the pericardial fluid was 3.5 U/l. Negative results were observed for serum anti-nuclear antibodies and tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen (CA) 125, CA 15-3 and CA 19-9. Serological tests for cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, mycoplasma, chlamydia, coxsackie virus, herpes simplex virus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis and toxoplasma were negative. In addition, direct examination of the pericardial fluid for mycobacteria, Aspergillus and yeast, as well as a pericardial fluid culture for bacteria, were negative. The drainage was maintained for 12 days. A repeated echocardiogram scan did not detect any pericardial effusion. The patient was readmitted after 20 days with pericardial tamponade, which required pericardiocentesis to be performed. A lemon-colored exudative fluid (600 ml) was removed and a catheter was maintained. The aforementioned etiological examinations were performed again, with all tests negative, with the exception of the enzyme-linked immunospot test (ELISPOT) for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. At day 48 following transplantation, a two-month period of empirical antituberculous therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide and moxifloxacin) was proposed, which was prolonged to three months. During this time period, the volume of pericardial drainage fluid remained at 200–600 ml per day. At day 77 following transplantation, a pericardial window with thoracic close drainage was performed due to the frequent obstruction of the catheter. Postoperative pericardial histopathological assessment revealed chronic inflammatory changes without any evidence of malignancy or tuberculosis. The culture of pericardial fluid tested negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis after 60 days. At day 127 following transplantation, a pericardiocentesis was performed again to replace the blocked thoracic close drainage with a catheter. The ELISPOT was repeated and negative results were achieved.

Case Information: A 12-year-old Arab boy presented with multiple exfoliated teeth. His oral hygiene was relatively better with gingival enlargement around erupting teeth. Most of his permanent anterior teeth were lost with severe bone destruction around his remaining teeth. His lower molars appeared floating without any bone support. There was severe palmar plantar keratosis with keratinization of the dorsal surface of his hands.
Diagnostic Tests: A periodontal examination recorded a score of 4 (deep pocket) in his molars and incisors.

Case Information: A 40-year-old, HIV-positive female presented with a 1-month history of an annular truncal eruption. She had been on highly active antiretroviral therapy (ART) for 1 year (efavirenz, lamivudine, and tenofovir) without trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis and had a CD4 count of 316 cells/mm3. Her rapid plasma reagin and Treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay were negative. The patient was commenced on oral steroids at 0.5 mg/kg and her ART was discontinued for a 2-week period. During this time her rash improved markedly and the prednisone was slowly tapered, but the rash recurred despite discontinuation of her ART. In addition to the presenting rash, she developed an intercurrent herpes zoster infection and was treated with antivirals. Subsequently, she began developing an erythematous rash involving the malar area, annular erythematous plaques on the trunk, specifically on the “V” of the neck, and on the upper limbs with targetoid lesions on the palms and vasculitic lesions on the limbs.
Diagnostic Tests: ANF was negative, and histology showed a lichenoid eruption with basal cell vacuolization and colloid bodies. Her repeat ANF remained negative with a low serum complement level C3 (0.7 g/L) and C4 (0.14 g/L) and a positive anti-Ro SSA antibody.

Case Information: A 21-year-old male with a recent history of gym membership and weightlifting presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of pain and swelling in the right upper limb. His past medical history includes COVID-19 infection 12 months ago, with no family history of thromboembolic conditions. Physical examination showed a swollen and erythematous right upper limb, with palpable peripheral pulses comparable to the left side. The range of motion in the right upper limb was intact. The left upper limb and both lower limbs appeared normal. There were no signs or symptoms indicative of pulmonary embolism.
Diagnostic Tests: Right upper limb POCUS was concerning for subclavian vein thrombus with a distended right subclavian vein. Blood work up revealed a non-negative D-dimer at 0.93 mg/l (reference range <0.50mg/l). His chest x-ray showed no obvious abnormalities, and no evidence of an accessory rib. An urgent formal ultrasound confirmed an acute 6 cm thrombus within the right subclavian vein. Furthermore, it showed normal compressibility and colour flow within the right basilic vein, brachial vein, cephalic vein and axillary vein without any evidence of thrombosis. The IR venogram showed an acute thrombotic occlusion of the right subclavian vein with a high-grade stenosis at the junction of the first rib and clavicle.

Case Information: A 24-year-old male (height: 169 cm, weight: 44 kg, blood pressure: 168/75 mmHg) presented with sudden episodes of consciousness disturbance and muscle spasms. He had a history of cerebral haemorrhage, with two previous incidents occurring between the ages of 23 and 24 years. He was an only child, and his parents had no history of haemorrhage or abnormal skin conditions. The patient was referred to the endocrinology department with multiple intracranial calcifications, acute intracerebral haemorrhage, and several other notable features. Diagnostic Tests: The results showed a missense mutation within exon 5 of LMNA (c.898G>C) that caused a substitution of aspartate 300 by histidine (p.Asp300His). There were no WRN mutations.

Case Information: A 59-year-old male presented with a history of progressive muscle weakness starting in his late twenties at the outpatient department of the rehabilitation center, Daejeon St. Mary's Hospital (Daejeon, Republic of Korea). He was born healthy at full-term and had no health issues during childhood and early adulthood, including completing mandatory national military training. In his late twenties, he experienced frequent falls and difficulty climbing stairs, with progressive muscle weakness primarily in the pelvic girdle and proximal legs, while the motor function of the upper extremities remained normal at that time. By the age of 38, he noticed muscle weakness in the upper extremities, a waddling gait, hyperlordosis of the lower back, and anterior pelvic tilt. His gait disturbance and muscle weakness continued to progress slowly. By the age of 55, he was unable to walk and required a wheelchair for mobility. His family history indicates a genetic background of autosomal recessive inheritance related to his muscle condition. One of his elder brothers exhibited similar symptoms and was diagnosed with progressive muscular dystrophy in his twenties. The patient is married to a healthy woman and has healthy children with no signs of muscle weakness.
Diagnostic Tests: The electrodiagnostic study revealed myopathy, normal values in the motor and sensory nerve conduction study, and short-amplitude muscle unit action potentials with early recruitment in needle electromyography. Quantitative electromyography also showed a myopathic pattern. In the laboratory findings, the serum creatine kinase (CK) level was elevated in 2042 IU/L.

Case Information: In July 2010, a 53-year-old woman with no significant neurologic history experienced a single convulsion. Four months later, she experienced two similar convulsions, quickly progressing to status epilepticus. She was treated at an outside institution and recovered full function and returned to work. Initial MR imaging at that time was reported as normal. Despite AED treatment, she continued to have focal seizures, characterized by clonic jerks of the right face. Over the next year, her seizures increased in both frequency and semiology, involving the right arm as well as language. Admission to an outside epilepsy monitoring unit (EMU) revealed both electroclinical (semiology of right face/arm movements) and purely electrographic seizures arising from the left frontal region in the context of minimal responsiveness, consistent with focal status epilepticus. She was again treated for status epilepticus and discharged on AED polytherapy: phenytoin, valproic acid, levetiracetam, and oxcarbazepine. As her epilepsy became more refractory, a very extensive etiologic work-up was performed at an outside institution, approximately 2 years from epilepsy onset.
Diagnostic Tests: MRI demonstrated a left parietal FLAIR hyperintensity with mild associated volume loss. Admission to an outside epilepsy monitoring unit (EMU) revealed both electroclinical (semiology of right face/arm movements) and purely electrographic seizures arising from the left frontal region in the context of minimal responsiveness, consistent with focal status epilepticus. Brain PET imaging performed showed overall left hemisphere hypometabolism, with areas of increased metabolism in the left frontal, parietal, and occipital regions. Extensive serum and CSF studies, notably paraneoplastic and autoimmune encephalitis antibody testing as well as genetic testing for CADASIL and MELAS were also negative. The biopsy showed only mild gliosis and rare T lymphocytes, without evidence of vasculitis, microglial nodules, or viral cytopathic changes.

Case Information: The patient is a 55-year-old woman with a history of muscle tightening episodes for over 10 years, primarily occurring at night. She also experiences a squeezing sensation in her feet, which is worsened by wearing shoes. These symptoms have progressively worsened, leading to medical evaluation. Neurological examination showed no abnormalities in mental status, cranial nerves, muscle strength, cerebellar function, or reflexes. Sensory examination for light touch, vibration, proprioception, pin prick, and temperature was normal. Her gait, tested with shoes, was tentative, indicating foot discomfort. No trophic changes were observed in her hands or feet. Neurophysiological testing indicated normal motor and sensory nerve conduction parameters. Needle electromyogram of selected leg muscles showed no abnormalities, and the study did not indicate any large fiber neuropathy.
Diagnostic Tests: Quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test showed significantly decreased sweat production in both proximal and distal segments of the right leg. Skin biopsy showed significant reduction in the epidermal nerve fiber density 0.93 (nl>8.3) in the distal thigh and 0.88 (nl>4.3) in the distal leg.

Case Information: A 42-year-old female presented with sudden, widespread hair loss from the scalp occurring over a 1-day period. The patient has a history of vitiligo vulgaris and has been receiving treatment with topical tacrolimus 0.1% ointment, fluticasone ointment, and spot Narrow-band UVB (NB-UVB) phototherapy for the past 8 months. She underwent an appendicectomy 1 month ago and subsequently developed cellulitis of the left hand.
Diagnostic Tests: Dermoscopy showed the presence of black dots, yellow dots, and short vellus hair.

Case Information: A 5-year-old male child presented with severe gingival attachment loss. The child, accompanied by parents, had no notable medical history. Over the past 2 months, the child experienced gingival bleeding and pain while chewing. Clinical oral examination showed full primary dentition, minimal plaque, moderate gingival inflammation, severe attachment loss around teeth 52, 53, 62, 63, 54, 55, 64, and 65, and a supernumerary tooth in the 51 and 61 region. Bleeding on probing was observed, and periodontal pockets around the first primary molars measured 5 mm with furcal involvement. Panoramic radiograph indicated severe generalized vertical and horizontal bone loss. A complete medical evaluation was conducted, revealing normal levels for complete blood count, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, coagulation factors, and T4 lymphocyte counts. Slight elevations were noted in absolute monocyte and neutrophil counts and erythrocyte sedimentation rates. Microbiological evaluation of unstimulated saliva identified both aerobic and anaerobic microorganisms.
Diagnostic Tests: This revealed the presence of A. actinomycetemcomitans and Porphyromonas gingivalis from tissue biopsy.

Case Information: A 22-year-old Hispanic woman, previously in good health, experienced a severe headache (8 out of 10 on the pain scale) and blurred vision over the past 5 days. She visited the ophthalmology clinic due to a significant reduction in vision in her right eye more than her left, which gradually worsened over the 5-day period and began to interfere with her daily activities. She did not report any flashes of light or floaters in either eye. Visual acuity testing showed 20/70 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures, as well as examinations of the conjunctivae, corneas, anterior chamber, and irises, were all normal. Upon dilation, the posterior chamber examination revealed optic nerve congestion and prepapilledema. There was also subretinal fluid beneath the maculae and around the optic nerves. She was referred to the hospital for further evaluation.
Diagnostic Tests: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain with contrast revealed generalized leptomeningeal enhancement with 'sugar-coating' or 'zuckerguss pattern' in her vermis region of cerebellum. Her orbital MRI showed increased signal thickening at the posterior aspect of globes and focal enhancements. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 150 mm H2O, glucose 58 mg/dL, protein 46 mg/dL, WBC 180 cells/μL, RBC count 25, lymphocytes 96%, neutrophils 3%, and macrophages 1%.

Case Information: A 59-year-old Caucasian woman presented with progressive visual impairment in both eyes, which began in her thirties. She reported no family history of eye disorders. Her best corrected visual acuity was measured at 0.6 LogMAR in the right eye and 0.4 LogMAR in the left eye using ETDRS charts. Examination of the anterior segment revealed normal findings in both eyes, with no crystal deposits observed at the corneal limbus. Intraocular pressure was recorded at 16 mmHg in both eyes. Fundus biomicroscopy showed extensive chorioretinal atrophy in both eyes, accompanied by multiple crystalline deposits primarily located at the edges of the atrophic areas. Scotopic and photopic full-field electroretinograms were significantly reduced, while the electrooculogram remained within normal limits.
Diagnostic Tests: Next Generation Sequencing unveiled two pathogenic variants in CYP4V2 (c.424_427 del (p.(Lys142Glyfs*8)) and c.173C>A (p.(Pro58Gln)).

Case Information: The patient is a 40-year-old male who presented with memory loss. On April 9, 2019, he visited a local hospital with symptoms including tremor, involuntary urination, and incoherent speech. On April 1, 2019, he experienced disorientation while driving on a familiar road to work, resulting in a minor car accident, and he could not recall the details of the incident. These symptoms appeared 2–3 days following the accident. He reported intermittent headaches and memory loss over the past 5 years. His medical history includes being an ex-smoker with a 10 pack-year history and heavy alcohol consumption, averaging 8–10 bottles of soju per week for approximately 15 years. There is no relevant family history of brain disorders. Both the patient and his wife confirmed that there were no external circumstances outside of his workplace that could lead to poisoning from toxic substances. A review of his medical records and the history from the Korean National Health Insurance Service over the past 10 years showed no evidence of acute poisoning from toxic substances, except for exposure to CO2 arc welding at his workplace. The patient also reported experiencing difficulty breathing during welding operations due to several enclosed spaces in the workplace.
Diagnostic Tests: The T2 weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images showed lesions with high signal intensity in the bilateral globus pallidus. Subtle high signal intensity lesions were also seen in the bilateral cerebral white matter. An approximately 3-mm vascular outpouching lesion was suspected in the anterior communicating artery from the images, with mild stenosis in the mid portion of the basilar artery. Multifocal acute infarction in the centrum semiovales, parietal lobes, and occipital lobes bilaterally. Both the size and shape of the ventricle were normal. No brain atrophy or abnormalities in the brain parenchyma were noted. A mild cerebral dysfunction was observed.
